claims.text: Iterative active-learning refinement of an EAM potential will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch to within 5% of ab initio benchmarks.
Targeting and recalibrating poorly represented regions of configuration space will improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
The proposed method applies to FeCoNiCrAl in disordered solid and supercooled-liquid states near melting.
Molecular-dynamics exploration with the current potential can identify configurations for further training.
Uncertainty quantification can identify configurations that are poorly represented by the current EAM potential.
Target configurations can be labeled with ab initio calculations and incorporated through iterative potential retraining.
An EAM potential can be iteratively recalibrated in the same manner as the cited active-learned deep neural-network potentials.
A free-energy deviation of 5% or less is an appropriate convergence criterion for stopping the refinement cycles.
The applicable temperature interval is 0.95 Tm to 1.05 Tm and covers both near-melting solid and liquid states.
Dynamically updated local atomic descriptors derived from uncertainty quantification will capture motifs underrepresented by the baseline EAM.
Active learning can include crystalline and liquid configurations in potential training and exploration.
Repeating MD exploration, configuration selection, ab initio labeling, and model updating will improve the free-energy integration path.
The refined EAM will reduce path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD's static EAM reference.
The refinement will improve phase-space overlap by approximately 50%.
The refined reference will achieve a free-energy deviation below 5%.
The standard TOR-TILD protocol uses an unrefined, static EAM reference potential.
The procedure is applicable across FeCoNiCrAl compositions near melting but requires validation before transfer to other alloy systems or distant temperature ranges.
The magnitude of mismatch reduction depends on the complexity of the ab initio landscape and the efficiency of the uncertainty-quantification strategy.
Failure to reach or consistently approach a 5% free-energy difference after refinement would falsify the hypothesis.
